newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgaria leader offers tougher line on crisis.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgaria leader offers tougher line on crisis.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president Petar Stoyanov, who takes office on Wednesday, promises a tougher approach than his predecessor to the country's political deadlock but months of instability may still lie ahead.

Stoyanov, a lawyer untainted by the country's communist past, has replaced Zhelev, a dissident philosopher who became president in August 1990 after former communist leader Todor Zhivkov was ousted in 1989.
Stoyanov decisively defeated the Socialist candidate in last November's presidential elections, but the Socialists now say the 44-year-old divorce lawyer is a president they can do business with.

"The Socialists long ago decided Zhelev was the enemy, and they spent seven years hating him. Against this background of irrational hatred for Zhelev, they think Stoyanov is more reasonable," said analyst Evgenii Dainov, director of the Centre for Social Practices.
After months of criticism of his handling of the economy, Zhan Videnov suddenly resigned as prime minister and party leader on December 21.
The Socialists have offered a general election by the end of the year, but the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) remains vehemently opposed to any interim government led by the Socialists.
"By nominating Petar Stoyanov as president, the UDF has elected the best of itself," said Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the Socialists' nominee for premier.

"He has the possibility to be not just a president but a head of state, to coordinate all positions, to think for the country. I am deeply convinced that he will not serve only one party but he will be a free president, led only by the interests of the state."

Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic where the president's powers are limited, but while Zhelev has dealt with the crisis by refusing to ask the Socialists to form a government in the interests of social peace, Stoyanov has begun mediation efforts between the Socialists and the UDF.

He has said he may give the Socialists a mandate to form a new government as the constitution requires, but in his inaugural speech at his swearing-in ceremony on Sunday backed the opposition's call for a quick general election.
"It has been obvious from the beginning that he will push things forward rather than conducting holding operations," Dainov said.
Diplomats describe Stoyanov's handling of the crisis as statesmanlike and say they expect him to take a much more active role within the powers of the presidency.
Under the post-communist constitution, the president is a mainly ceremonial figure with limited powers.

Real power lies with parliament but the president represents Bulgaria in international relations, appoints ambassadors, judges and certain other officials, and has limited veto powers over laws passed by parliament.

The Socialists have 125 seats in the 240-seat parliament and their majority looks increasingly fragile with the foundation of a rival leftist coalition and the loss of support from their one-time allies in the Bulgarian Business Bloc.
Other Socialist deputies may oppose the appointment of Dobrev as premier, as his post gives him access to information on business and other activities which could discredit them.
If the Socialists' cabinet fails to win parliamentary approval, then Stoyanov should ask the UDF, the next biggest party in parliament, to form a government.

The UDF has said it will not form a minority government under the present parliament. Any short-term government would be unlikely to win a desperately-needed new accord from the International Monetary Fund to avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.
Under the constitution, if all parties in parliament fail to form a government, the president appoints a caretaker government, dissolves parliament, and schedules elections within two months.
The IMF has proposed a tough fixed exchange rate regime as a last resort to shore up the crumbling economy but further negotiations are on hold until a new government is formed.
Outgoing Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov has promised to meet January's payments on its Brady bonds, but a quick solution is needed as the next big payment is due in July.

Bulgarian Brady bonds were firmer on the secondary debt market on Monday, but traders said this had more to do with the high yield they offer than with any signs of improvement in Bulgaria's own situation.
